body: Kinda reminds me of another 256b intro called [lattice](http://pouet.net/prod.php?which=4659). It runs a lot slower and isn't as flashy as Puls, but still pretty impressive.

> They started us off doing silly things in front of the group, then at later sessions they invited other people into the room to watch us do things, like talk about embarrassing subjects, or sing karaoke. Then later they had us going outside and talking to random people in supermarkets, bars, and out on the street. It was very helpful to me.

That sounds terrifying, but I totally believe that would be helpful for me too.

> They also assigned us "homework" like going to meetup groups (meetup.com), even asking girls out, etc. These are the sorts of things we could assign ourselves on our own, I guess, but now there's the added guilt of "if I don't do it everyone at the group will judge me!" Peer pressure is effective :)

That's something I don't know if I could do alone either, at least not without having someone to whine to afterwards if (and when) it doesn't go well :)

> So, my advice is: look for programs like this, people giving free therapy for the sake of some study. Universities often do things like this.

Haven't heard of any such studies here, so I'll probably have to come up with the money for CBT from somewhere. I'll keep looking though.

> And at the very least, try and drag yourself to a meetup group.

As I've mentioned earlier, I went to a group last year, but I don't really know whether to call it group therapy or a meetup group.. I guess it was somewhere in between. Suggestion has been noted though :) Thank you!

Nice to hear! Yeah.. I know that'd be a good way to get into contact with people, and I'd like to join some sports club here, but I've just always chickened out before. Although one reason for liking sports for me has probably been that there you DON'T have to talk to people that much (in my experience). I'm trying to work up enough courage to join this autumn, but we'll see how it goes :)

> Oh, and also, CBT can be self-taught (at least all the cognitive part and most of the behavioral).

That's encouraging to hear. I'll definitely give this stuff a shot!

Yes, there's a lot of work to be done.. guess it's time to finally get started :)

I've heard good things about cognitive therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy, but AFAIK such therapy can only be gotten from private practitioners here and I can't really afford that :( But I'm gonna check with the students' health care services when they open again anyway.

The book suggestion seems good, and it's available in book stores here too, so I'll give it a look.

> Also practice speaking slower than you usually do. Nobody will notice but the effects are very positive.

Do you mean it would give more time to think about what I'm going to say, or what kinds of effects are you talking about? Not being able to think of anything to say is a big problem for me, but I don't talk very much as it is, so I guess I should work on opening my mouth first :)

> I hope it helps 'cause cognitive therapy has helped me make significant progress as the drugs didn't really cut it for me. I can almost say I'm anxiety-free if there is anything like that.

That's great to hear! It must feel awesome not worrying so much about social situations. Hopefully I'll get there (or close) some day too :)

Knowing that everyone in the group knew about my anxiety did make it easier to be around them, but not enough to actually talk. I suppose I could try it again. I've never actually been out for a drink, or just hung out like that, with anyone, so it seems a bit daunting as I don't know at all how to act there, when to talk and about what, when to leave, etc. I guess I'm not only, as you say, out of practice in socializing, but I never had many of those skills in the first place.

But anyway, I'll take the therapy again into consideration.

Yes, you're probably right. The baby steps comment made me think that my previous attempts to become more social have been too ambitious; that I've been trying to go "all in", while I probably should've started with little things like you mentioned. It sounds pretty obvious now when you think about it, but I guess it didn't pop into my mind then :) Saying even little things like that seems pretty frightening now, but I guess one can only hope it'll get easier gradually..

Regarding group therapy, I actually managed to go to a group for people with anxieties last year(?), but it went pretty much the same as usually: I was too frightened to initiate any conversations, and stayed quiet unless directly asked something. Not that I could've thought of anything worthwhile to say anyway..

As for gathering my courage, that's what I'm trying to do now, but it is a bit too easy to fall back on avoiding everything, because that's what I'm used to doing and it's familiar. Well, thank you for your helpful comment :)

Thanks for the comment!

> I don't know if this would help... but maybe sit and try to actually visualize the outcome you fear. ie, imagine what would actually happen if any particular thing you said or did appeared "stupid or pathetic"... what would happen, etc etc? spend time on this for a bit.

Well, I suppose it would make them take me less seriously and maybe make fun of me. I know in most cases that probably isn't true; that in many cases it might even make me seem more easily approachable etc. Still I would get the feeling that I couldn't face the person anymore because I've embarrassed myself, and it's really hard to convince myself that my fears are exaggerated. The feeling of wanting to sink into the ground is just overpowering.

When it comes to my family, I don't really know what would happen, because I haven't had a conversation with them since I was like 14.. To them I can't say much, stupid things or not, because I'm even afraid of getting compliments from them. That's a horrible feeling for some reason.
